title: The bowl of oil
hookLine: carry a full bowl of oil past a crowd and a dancing beauty, a swordsman behind you (SN 47.20)

lines: A BOWL FULL TO THE BRIM.
cards: A huge crowd is gathering in the town square. Word has spread: the most beautiful woman in the land is here, and she's dancing and singing. People are pushing to see.

Now a man is handed a bowl filled to the very brim with oil, and told to carry it straight through the middle of all that, between the crowd and the dancer. Behind him walks another man, with a drawn sword.
Spill one drop, he's told, and you lose your head.

teach.b: The Buddha tells this at Sedaka, the same town as the acrobats, and asks his monks a simple question. Would that man stop paying attention to the bowl, and let his eyes drift to the dancer? No, sir, they say.
Then he says what the picture means.

teach.h: THE BOWL: MINDFULNESS OF THE BODY.
teach.b: The bowl of oil filled to the brim stands for mindfulness of the body. So train yourselves, he says, to develop mindfulness of the body, to make it your vehicle and your ground. The picture is extreme on purpose.
The crowd and the dancer are everything that pulls attention outward: the alerts, the drama, the bright, loud, lovely things.

teach.h: THE SWORD: THE STAKES ARE REAL.
teach.b: The sutta doesn't explain the sword, but one way to read it is as the seriousness of the stakes. Not that distraction is a crime; just that it may cost more than it seems.
And the bowl is the body itself: the breath, the feet, the hands, right here, the thing you're already carrying. The man doesn't shut his eyes. He doesn't stay home.

teach.h: THROUGH THE CROWD, NOT AROUND IT.
teach.b: He walks straight through the crowd while the music plays.
The practice isn't avoiding life; it's carrying something steady through the middle of it.
That's right mindfulness at its most physical: attention in your hands, at the brim of the bowl, step by step, while everything around you invites you to look away.

how: Many Buddhists practice mindfulness of the body in walking meditation and daily tasks, and some teachers have students carry a full cup or bowl slowly as a training in steady attention.

o: mindfulness of the body, felt steadily
a healing practice for bodily illness
a trance where the body is forgotten

games.q: the bowl of oil: tap the pairs.
p: the same town as the acrobats

s: the man avoids the crowd by taking another route
he walks straight between the crowd and the dancer.
the brim-full bowl stands for mindfulness of the body
the Buddha says so, then tells the monks to train in it.
the practice the simile teaches is avoiding busy places
it's carrying something steady through the middle of them.

games.q: you're carrying a bowl of oil full to the brim. the crowd roars: the dancer has started. a man with a sword walks behind you. what do you do?
o: glance at the dancer, just once.
keep your attention on the bowl.
set the bowl down and watch.
games.why: the monks answer that the man wouldn't neglect the bowl for a moment; the Buddha says the bowl is mindfulness of the body.

practice: If you can, fill a cup to the top and hold it, or imagine one in your hands, and slowly carry it a few steps, or raise and lower it, without spilling.
Notice how the whole body gathers around the brim, the breath slowing, the hands softening, then set it down and sit with that same steadiness.

wordCard.voice: Kayagata sati, mindfulness of the body. The Buddha's image for mindfulness of the body: carried brim-full through the crowd, without spilling.

orig.note: Pali kāyagatā sati: mindfulness directed to the body, which the brim-full bowl stands for.

carryVoice: Your line: don't spill. The bowl is the body you're already carrying. That's day three hundred ninety-one.
